etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English cley, clay, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”), from Proto-West Germanic *klaij, from Proto-Germanic *klajjaz (“clay”), from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to glue, paste, stick together”).

Cognate with Dutch klei (“clay”), Low German Klei (“clay”), German Klei, Danish klæg (“clay”); compare Ancient Greek γλία (glía), Latin glūten (“glue”) (whence ultimately English glue), Russian глина (glina, “clay”). Related also to clag, clog.

definitions.definition: A mineral substance made up of small crystals of silica and alumina, that is ductile when moist; the material of pre-fired ceramics.

quote.citation: 1914 November, Louis Joseph Vance, “An Outsider […]”, in Munsey’s Magazine, volume LIII, number II, New York, N.Y.: The Frank A[ndrew] Munsey Company, […], published 1915, →OCLC, chapter I (Anarchy), page 377, column 2:
quote.text: Three chairs of the steamer type, all maimed, comprised the furniture of this roof-garden, with (by way of local color) on one of the copings a row of four red clay flower-pots filled with sun-baked dust  […]

definitions.definition: An earth material with ductile qualities.
(tennis) A tennis court surface made of crushed stone, brick, shale, or other unbound mineral aggregate.
(biblical) The material of the human body.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Job 10:8-9:
quote.text: Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about...thou hast made me as the clay.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 64:8:
quote.text: But now, O Lord, thou art our Father; we are the clay, and thou art our potter; and we are the work of thy hand.

definitions.definition: (geology) A particle less than 3.9 microns in diameter, following the Wentworth scale.
A clay pipe for smoking tobacco.
(Internet slang, humorous) Land or territory of a country or other political region, especially when subject to territorial claims.
(transitive) To add clay to, to spread clay onto.
(transitive, of sugar) To purify using clay.

quote.citation: 1776, Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 7: Of Colonies, Part 2: Causes of Prosperity of New Colonies,
quote.text: They amounted, therefore, to a prohibition, at first of claying or refining sugar for any foreign market, and at present of claying or refining it for the market, which takes off, perhaps, more than nine-tenths of the whole produce.

quote.citation: 1985, Stuart B. Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society: Bahia, 1550-1835‎[1], page 200:
quote.text: The Portuguese had mastered the technique of claying sugar, and other European nations tried to learn the secrets from them.
